hints: For TLC, think about what two distances you can measure on the plate after the run, one for the spot and one for the solvent front.
For GLC, think about the journey of a sample, starting at the moment it is injected and ending when it reaches the detector.
walkthrough:
Picture what $R_f$ compares in TLC**
Imagine your TLC plate after development. You see a pencil baseline, a spot part way up, and a line where the solvent stopped. $R_f$ is simply a ratio that tells you how far the spot travelled relative to the solvent. So you measure from the baseline to the centre of the spot, then divide by the distance from the baseline to the solvent front.

Picture what retention time measures in GLC**
Now switch to a gas chromatography column. You inject the mixture at time zero and each component travels through at a different speed. The detector draws a peak when each one comes out. Retention time is just that waiting time from injection to the top of the peak for that component.

Final answer: $R_f$ value = distance moved by component / spot / solute divided by distance moved by solvent front.
retention time = time between injection of sample and detection of component.

hints: Recall that in TLC the plate is solid so the moving liquid must be a solvent, while in GLC the moving carrier is a gas so the stationary coating must be a liquid that will not evaporate.
walkthrough:
Match the phase to the technique**
In TLC the stationary phase is already fixed as a thin solid layer of silica or alumina on the plate, so the box you fill in is the mobile phase. That has to be a liquid solvent that can climb by capillary action, it can be polar or non-polar depending on the separation needed.
In gas/liquid chromatography the mobile phase is already fixed as an inert carrier gas such as helium, so the box you fill in is the stationary phase. That has to be a liquid that stays put at high oven temperature, so a non-volatile liquid with a high boiling point coated inside the column.

Final answer: thin-layer chromatography mobile phase: polar or non-polar solvent, e.g. ethanol or hexane.
gas/liquid chromatography stationary phase: non-volatile / high boiling point liquid coated on solid support.

hints: Remember that a larger $R_f$ means the spot travelled further up the plate with the solvent, so think about whether A spent more time dissolved in the moving solvent or stuck on the solid.
walkthrough:
Link distance travelled to intermolecular attractions**
Think of TLC as a competition. The solid silica attracts molecules and holds them back, while the rising solvent dissolves them and drags them forward. If A ends up higher with a larger $R_f$, A must have favoured the moving solvent. In particle terms, A is more soluble in the mobile phase and less strongly adsorbed onto the polar stationary phase than B, so it spends more time moving and travels further in the same time.
Final answer: A is more soluble in the mobile phase OR A has less adsorption / weaker attraction to the stationary phase, so it is carried further.

hints: Draw out Y as $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ and Z as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and look for symmetry and equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2$ groups.
walkthrough:
Count unique proton environments**
Label the structures fully. Y is hexane-2,5-dione, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$. The molecule is symmetrical through the centre of the $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ bond. The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are identical to each other, and the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups are identical to each other. That gives 2 distinct environments, so 2 peaks.
Z is heptan-3-one with an extra carbonyl, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ drawn as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$? Actually the diagram shows $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ symmetrical isomer, more simply 3,5? Check symmetry: left and right $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ groups are mirror images, and the central $\text{CH}_2$ between two $\text{C=O}$ groups is unique? Wait, look carefully: Z has $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$? No, the image is heptane-3,4-dione, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Left $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ matches right $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. So again only 2 types of protons, the $\text{CH}_3$ protons are all equivalent and the $\text{CH}_2$ protons are all equivalent. That also gives 2 peaks.

Final answer: Y: 2 peaks observed.
Z: 2 peaks observed.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule by counting protons on adjacent carbons for each environment in Y and Z.
Notice that carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ carbons carry no protons, so they block coupling between groups on either side.
walkthrough:
Work out splitting in Y**
Take Y, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$. Focus on the $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{C=O}$. The neighbouring carbon is the carbonyl carbon with zero protons, so n = 0, n+1 = 1, a singlet. Focus on the $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ on one side and $\text{CH}_2$ on the other side. But the two $\text{CH}_2$ groups are chemically equivalent by symmetry, protons within the same environment do not split each other. Effectively each $\text{CH}_2$ sees zero non-equivalent neighbours, so it is also a singlet. Hence two singlets.

Work out splitting in Z**
Take Z, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Focus on the $\text{CH}_3$ group. Its neighbour is $\text{CH}_2$ with 2 protons, so n = 2, n+1 = 3, a triplet. Focus on the $\text{CH}_2$ group. Its neighbour is $\text{CH}_3$ with 3 protons, the carbonyl side has no protons, so n = 3, n+1 = 4, a quartet. Hence one triplet plus one quartet.

Final answer: Y: two singlets.
Z: one triplet and one quartet.
